questions.question_text: It is estimated that what percent of eighth graders have tried illicit drugs?
questions.explanation: It is estimated that approximately 20 percent of eighth graders in the United States have tried illicit drugs, and about 30 percent of tenth through twelfth graders have used an illicit substance[cite: 12]. Alcohol remains the most common substance used and abused by adolescents[cite: 12]. Binge drinking occurs in about 6 percent of adolescents, and teens with alcohol use disorders are at greater risk of problems with other substances as well[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about adolescent substance abuse is true?

options.text: Substance use among adolescents does not differ between males and females.
White and Hispanic students are less likely than African American students to report lifetime alcohol use and heavy episodic use.
White and Hispanic students are less likely than African-American students to report both lifetime and current marijuana use.
“Experimenters” who are more likely to progress to substance use disorders are youth with multiple risk factors.

correct_answer.text: “Experimenters” who are more likely to progress to substance use disorders are youth with multiple risk factors.

correct_answers.text: “Experimenters” who are more likely to progress to substance use disorders are youth with multiple risk factors.

questions.explanation: “Experimenters” who are more likely to progress to substance use disorders are youth with multiple risk factors[cite: 12]. The literature on the development of substance use and substance use disorders in adolescents has identified an assortment of individual, peer, family, and community risk factors[cite: 12]. Within a developmental context, genetic predispositions to affective, cognitive, and behavioral dysregulation are exacerbated by family and peer factors in addition to the normative developmental issues of puberty, leading to substance use and pathological use[cite: 12]. Both temperament and social interactions (i.e., family, peer relations) have a critical role in outcomes of adolescent substance use disorder[cite: 12]. A number of family factors have been implicated as increasing the risk of substance use disorder in children and adolescents[cite: 12]. Family environment and the extent to which youth feel supported and connected to their families of origin can have protective influences on treatment outcomes for teens[cite: 12]. Some of the most widely recognized familial risk factors include the nature of bonding, parental supervision, discipline style, and adherence to religious practices[cite: 12]. Affiliation with socially deviant peers has been shown in many studies to promote substance use[cite: 12]. Affiliation with older peers may be especially hazardous because of premature exposure to risky situations, including drugs, sex, automobile travel, and otherwise problematic social settings without adult supervision[cite: 12]. Although general indices of peer support suggest a detrimental effect on teen substance use, having nonusing social supports in youth social networks has been shown to be predictive of abstinence posttreatment[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: Which of these psychiatric disorders is most commonly associated with substance abuse in adolescents?
questions.explanation: A number of psychiatric disorders are commonly comorbid with adolescent substance abuse, including conduct disorder, oppositional-defiant disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), dysthymia, major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, posttraumatic stress disorder, social phobia, bulimia nervosa, and schizophrenia[cite: 12]. Of these, conduct disorder is most commonly associated with substance use disorders in adolescents, with studies suggesting rates of conduct disorder ranging from 50 to 80 percent among adolescents with substance abuse or dependence[cite: 12]. Although ADHD is commonly observed in adolescents who abuse drugs or alcohol, the observed association is likely attributable to the high comorbidity between conduct disorder and ADHD[cite: 12]. Early onset of conduct disorder and comorbidity with ADHD likely increases the risk for later substance abuse[cite: 12]. Generalized anxiety disorder and schizophrenia, although less common than conduct disorder and ADHD in the adolescent population, are also associated with adolescent substance abuse[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: Which of the following psychiatric symptoms commonly co-occur with adolescent substance use disorders?
questions.explanation:
Substantial evidence supports the presence of substance use disorder as a risk factor for adolescent suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, and completed suicides[cite: 12]. This relationship may be partly explained by the acute and chronic effects of substances; adolescents who attempt or complete suicide are often under the influence of substances when engaging in suicidal behavior[cite: 12]. Acute effects of substances may include intensely dysphoric states, disinhibition, impaired judgment, increased impulsivity, and may exacerbate underlying anxiety, mood, or psychotic symptoms[cite: 12]. Aggressive behaviors are also manifest in many adolescents with substance use disorders[cite: 12]. Consumption of particular substances, such as alcohol, amphetamines, cocaine, and phencyclidine (PCP), may increase the likelihood of aggression[cite: 12]. The direct pharmacological effects of these substances may be enhanced by preexisting psychopathology, mixing of substances, and relative inexperience of adolescent substance users[cite: 12].
Studies of clinical populations indicate high rates of anxiety disorders among adolescent substance abusers, with estimated rates ranging from 7 to 40 percent[cite: 12]. The temporal relationship between anxiety symptoms and substance abuse varies; whereas social phobia symptoms often precede substance use, panic attacks may follow the onset of substance use[cite: 12]. Adolescents with substance abuse are commonly found to have histories of traumatic exposure and symptoms such as reexperiencing, emotional numbing, and avoidance, underlining the relationship between substance use disorders and posttraumatic stress disorder[cite: 12]. The bingeing and purging behaviors of bulimia nervosa are also common in teens with substance use disorders[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding adolescent substance abuse is true?

options.text: Use of marijuana is the strongest predictor of future cocaine use.
Prevalence rates for cocaine use are currently lower among adolescents than among adolescents in the 1990s.
Children of alcohol abusers have a 25 percent chance of themselves developing alcohol abuse.
Inhalants are most commonly used by younger adolescents, and their use declines with age.

questions.explanation: Marijuana is often referred to as a “gateway drug” because it is the most widely used illicit drug among adolescents, and marijuana use increases the likelihood of using additional drugs; for example, marijuana use is the strongest predictor of future cocaine use[cite: 12]. The Monitoring the Future 2010 Survey indicates that prevalence rates of cocaine use among adolescents remain at lower levels than were reported in the 1990s[cite: 12]. Unlike most other substances, inhalants are most commonly used by younger adolescents, and their use declines with age[cite: 12]. Commonly used inhalants include glue, aerosols, and gasoline[cite: 12]. Family transmission of risk for alcoholism is well established; children of alcohol abusers have been reported to have a 25 percent chance of developing alcohol abuse themselves[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about adolescents and adults with substance use disorders is true?

options.text: Relapse in adults is primarily influenced by social pressure for use, but in adolescents, situations involving negative affect more strongly contribute to relapse.
Compared with adults, adolescents have a lower level of return to substance use after treatment.
Adolescents are no likelier to experience noxious or adverse reactions to substances than more experienced adult users.
Comorbid conduct disorder in adolescents with substance use disorders predicts lower rates of treatment completion and future abstinence.

correct_answer.text: Comorbid conduct disorder in adolescents with substance use disorders predicts lower rates of treatment completion and future abstinence.

correct_answers.text: Comorbid conduct disorder in adolescents with substance use disorders predicts lower rates of treatment completion and future abstinence.

questions.explanation:
Adolescents in substance abuse treatment programs as a group tend to have begun substance use at early ages, progress rapidly to use of “hard” drugs, and use multiple substances[cite: 12]. Other clinical features of adolescents entering treatment often include high rates of comorbid psychiatric disorders; deviant behavior; school difficulties, including truancy; family disruption; and substance abuse in family members[cite: 12].
Data indicate that many adolescents return to some level of alcohol or drug abuse after treatment[cite: 12]. Specific predictors of outcome after treatment have been identified, including patient characteristics, social support system variables, and treatment program characteristics[cite: 12]. Psychopathology that predated the onset of substance abuse, particularly conduct disorder, predicts lower rates of treatment completion and future abstinence[cite: 12]. Although factors such as the severity of substance use may predict short-term treatment outcomes, longer term outcomes may depend more on social and environmental factors[cite: 12]. For example, studies suggest that relapse in adolescence is frequently associated with social pressure to use, but in adults, relapse is commonly tied to situations involving negative affect (not vice versa)[cite: 12]. Attendance at support or aftercare groups, which can be sources of peer support as teens attempt abstinence, is associated with higher rates of abstinence and other measures of positive outcome among adolescents compared with youth who do not attend such groups[cite: 12].
Adolescents have higher rates of return to substance use after treatment than adults (not vice versa)[cite: 12]. Nevertheless, treatment has been demonstrated to have beneficial effects on teens, with positive outcomes including decreased interpersonal conflict, improved academic achievement, and increased participation in social and occupational activities[cite: 12].
Adolescent substance users are more likely than adults to have minimal tolerance to substances; thus, they may experience more noxious or adverse reactions to substances compared with more experienced adult users[cite: 12]. Inexperienced teen users may not appreciate the extent of their intoxication or the deleterious effects of substance use on their overall functioning[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: Successful substance abuse prevention programs appear to be those that

options.text: take into account the socioeconomic and cultural realities of targeted communities

questions.explanation: Prevention efforts are based on theoretical models of the etiology of adolescent substance use and abuse[cite: 12]. Most prevention interventions are based on social learning models, or changing what young people see and learn in their environments produces behavioral changes[cite: 12]. These interventions often include educational approaches, addressing three primary factors: (1) knowledge and attitude, (2) values and decision making, and (3) social competency and skills[cite: 12]. Family-based outreach (e.g., parent training) and community-based projects (advocacy groups, media campaigns, and regulatory changes) are also critical aspects of comprehensive prevention efforts[cite: 12]. Successful prevention programs seem to be those that target salient risk factors, teach skills, provide adequate follow-up, and take into account the socioeconomic and cultural realities of targeted communities[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: The treatments of choice for alcohol abuse in adolescents includes all of the following except
questions.explanation: Treatment programs for adolescents with alcohol abuse contain a number of basic components, including individual psychotherapy, a self-help group setting, drug-specific counseling, and relapse prevention efforts[cite: 12]. These may be combined in any of a number of inpatient or outpatient programs[cite: 12]. Disulfiram and acamprosate are not current treatments of choice for adolescents with alcohol abuse[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: Risk factors for the development of adolescent substance abuse include all of the following except
questions.explanation: Risk factors for the development of alcohol or drug abuse include an early onset of cigarette smoking, diminished parental supervision, parental substance abuse, and conduct disorder[cite: 12]. Pervasive developmental disorder is not thought to be a risk factor for substance abuse[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: The four leading causes of death among young people age 15 to 24 years, all of which are correlated with substance abuse, include all of the following except
questions.explanation: The leading causes of death among young people ages 15 to 24 years are, in order, motor vehicle accidents (MVAs) (37 percent), homicide (14 percent), suicide (12 percent), and non-MVA accidents (12 percent)[cite: 12]. These events are frequently correlated with both the acute and chronic effects of alcohol and drug use among teenagers and young adults[cite: 12]. Thirty percent of adolescents brought to a pediatric trauma center have evidence of involvement with drugs and alcohol[cite: 12]. Cancer is not one of the four leading causes of death in this age group and does not commonly correlate with substance abuse in adolescents and young adults[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: For 10- to 18-year old students, most diverted opiates analgesics come from
questions.explanation: In a study of 10- to 18-year old children and adolescents, students reported the sources of diverted opiate analgesics are greater than 33 percent from family and approximately 17 percent from friends[cite: 12]. Diversion and misuse are common in both high school and college populations[cite: 12]. Opioid analgesics are the most widely prescribed and the most widely abused drugs[cite: 12]. Stimulants and sedative or anxiety medications have the highest ratios of illicit versus medical use[cite: 12].

questions.question_text: The only category in the text revision of the fourth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-IV-TR) in which caffeine is included
questions.explanation: Substance dependence refers to a cluster of cognitive, behavioral, and sometimes physiological symptoms that accompany the continued heavy use of a substance[cite: 12]. There is a pattern of repeated use that results in tolerance, withdrawal, and compulsive self-administration[cite: 12]. Substance abuse refers to a maladaptive pattern of substance use leading to a clinically significant amount of distress within a 12-month period[cite: 12]. The impairment may take the form of decreased performance in school or work, or it may lead to physical danger or legal problems[cite: 12]. Substance intoxication is a reversible syndrome caused by use of a substance in which clinically significant behavioral or psychological changes occur[cite: 12]. The only DSM-IV-TR disorder that includes caffeine is substance intoxication[cite: 12]. Substance withdrawal refers to a substance-specific syndrome caused by the cessation or reduction in use of a substance causing distress and impairment[cite: 12].
